summary: This informational document lists requirements for a mechanism that lets a Path Computation Client dynamically and automatically discover Path Computation Elements, along with information useful for choosing among them. Solutions are expected to meet these requirements.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 4674 lists what a mechanism for finding network path calculators must do. It covers the information clients need, who may receive it, how changes are reported, and how the discovery process is secured and managed.

subtitle: Requirements for clients to discover path-computation elements and choose among them.

tldr.problem: A Path Computation Client needs to know which Path Computation Elements are available, where they are, and which domains and functions they support. Manual configuration can be cumbersome and cannot report changes automatically.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 4674 requires discovery of basic PCE location, domains, functions, scope and changes, with optional detailed capability information and alternate PCEs.
tldr.outcome: It is an Informational requirements document, not a discovery protocol. Solutions are expected to satisfy its functional, security, scalability and management requirements.

today: RFC 4674 is an Informational requirements document published in October 2006. The unit metadata lists no RFC that updates or obsoletes it, and it does not define a discovery protocol.

sections.title: Why PCE Discovery Is Needed
sections.content:
A Path Computation Element (PCE) computes a traffic-engineered path from a network graph and constraints. A Path Computation Client (PCC) requests a path from a PCE; a PCE can also act as a client when it asks another PCE for a computation.

A domain may contain several PCEs for load sharing, backup, different capabilities, or inter-domain work. A PCC configured manually with every PCE can become difficult to maintain and cannot automatically detect a PCE appearing, changing or becoming unavailable.
sections.plainLanguage: A requesting device needs to find the network computer that can calculate a suitable path. Manual lists can become outdated when path calculators are added, changed or removed.

sections.title: Information a Discovery Mechanism Shares
sections.content:
General information is mandatory: a PCE's IPv4 or IPv6 address, the domains where it has visibility and can compute paths, and its inter-domain functions. Domains may be identified by an IGP area or an autonomous-system number.

Detailed information is optional. It may include supported path constraints, objective functions, ability to compute diverse or bidirectional paths, request limits, computing capacity, or alternate PCEs. The RFC leaves the exact definitions of these capabilities to other documents.
sections.plainLanguage: Every discovered path calculator must provide its address and the network areas it can use. The system may also share details about what it can do and which other calculator can replace it.

sections.title: Discovery Scope and Change Detection
sections.content:
Operators must be able to control which PCCs can learn about each PCE. The allowed scope includes PCCs in an IGP area, adjacent areas, an autonomous system, a set of autonomous systems, or selected PCCs across those systems. Discovery must be configurable and deactivatable for each PCE.

The mechanism must report new PCEs, changes to known information, and deactivation or failure. Real-time detection is not required; the RFC says discovery should be possible within a range of 60 seconds, with a configurable delay. Policies must control what information crosses domain boundaries.
sections.plainLanguage: Operators decide which clients may learn about each path calculator and what details they may receive. Clients should learn about changes or failures within a configurable period, with a target range of 60 seconds.

sections.title: Security and Scale Requirements
sections.content:
The RFC identifies threats including impersonating a PCE, reading or altering discovery information, disclosing it to unauthorized clients, and denial of service. A mechanism must authenticate and protect the integrity and confidentiality of information, limit its scope to authorized PCCs, and support an explicit trust model. PCEs and PCCs need globally unique identifiers.

The mechanism must scale with the number of clients, PCEs and domains without harming routing or signaling. The RFC gives minimum operational orders of magnitude of 1000 PCCs discovering one PCE and 100 PCEs discovered by one PCC. It also requires extensibility for future PCE information.
sections.plainLanguage: Messages about path calculators must be protected from fakes, changes and unauthorized readers. The mechanism also needs to support many clients and calculators without disrupting other network traffic.

sections.title: Configuration and Monitoring
sections.content:
Operators must be able to enable or disable discovery on both PCCs and PCEs. Automatic discovery must not prevent local configuration from adding information. The RFC requires MIB modules for controlling discovery on clients and PCEs.

The modules should expose discovered information, local configuration, active policies and change timing. Operators must also be able to monitor protocol operation and limit the effect of frequent changes, including the rate of announcements and the conditions that make a PCC switch to another PCE.
sections.plainLanguage: Operators need controls to turn automatic discovery on or off and add local information. They must also be able to inspect activity and limit disruptive updates.
